lesson.title: Releasing the Heat: Inside Exothermic Reactions
lesson.summary: In an exothermic reaction, the products end up with lower chemical potential energy than the reactants, and that difference in energy is released to the surroundings as heat.
lesson.body:
An exothermic reaction is one that releases energy, most commonly as heat, to its surroundings as it proceeds. This happens because the chemical potential energy stored in the bonds of the products is lower than the potential energy stored in the bonds of the reactants. Since energy cannot simply vanish, that difference has to leave the system somehow, and it leaves primarily as heat, often felt directly as the reaction container or the surrounding air warming up.

This connects to the more basic idea that any chemical change involves breaking old bonds in the reactants and forming new bonds in the products. Breaking a bond always requires an input of energy, while forming a bond always releases energy. In an exothermic reaction, the energy released when the new, more stable product bonds form is greater than the energy that had to be invested to break the original reactant bonds in the first place. That leftover surplus is what exits the system as heat, exactly as the conservation of energy principle from thermodynamics requires.

The combustion of methane in a gas stove is a familiar example: the reactants, methane and oxygen, hold more potential energy than the products, carbon dioxide and water, and the difference is given off as the heat and light of the flame, which is what actually warms the pot sitting on top of it. A chemical hand warmer offers a slower, gentler version of the same idea: iron powder inside the packet reacts gradually with oxygen from the air, and although the reaction is far less dramatic than a flame, it steadily releases enough heat over several hours to keep a pair of cold hands warm, because the reacting chemicals are continuously dumping energy into their surroundings, which in this case includes your hands.

It is worth being precise here: being exothermic says nothing on its own about how fast a reaction happens. Rate and energy release are separate ideas entirely, governed by different factors covered in earlier chapters on kinetics. Iron rusting is exothermic but proceeds slowly over days or weeks, while methane burning is exothermic and extremely fast once ignited. A reaction can release a great deal of energy overall while still taking a very long time to do it, or release energy almost instantly, depending entirely on factors like activation energy and collision frequency, not on whether it is exothermic.
